The observations point to the presence of two distinct compounds that have identical molecular masses but slightly different physical properties. In the ¹H NMR spectrum, the alpha-proton appears as two peaks of equal intensity with similar chemical shifts, ruling out spin–spin coupling. LC-MS at elevated temperature resolves two peaks of equal intensity, both showing the same mass spectrum consistent with the target molecule. 

Enantiomers (C) would not be distinguishable by standard NMR or achiral LC-MS. A precursor contaminant (A) would likely have a different mass. "Double coupling" (B) would typically yield a product with a different mass. The most plausible explanation is that the crude product is a mixture of diastereomers (D), which often form during peptide synthesis due to epimerization at the alpha-carbon. Diastereomers have identical masses but can be separated by chromatography and exhibit distinct NMR chemical shifts, especially for protons near the stereogenic center.

Answer: D
